body_markdown:
Barely two months after a 1996 F50[set a record](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/monthly-market-report-august-2026/) for Ferrari’s F1-derived supercar, another contender for the title of World’s Most Expensive F50 has appeared: A 106-mile example headed to Broad Arrow’s auction at the Wynn Las Vegas on Saturday, October 31.


Any Ferrari supercar with a naturally aspirated V-12 is going to get an enthusiast’s heart fluttering. An F50 might make them sit down. Essentially Ferrari’s 50th birthday present to itself, this carbon-bodied supercar draws extensively from contemporary F1 technology: The monocoque is made of carbon fiber, and the 513-hp, 4.7-liter V-12 engine, developed from the 3.5-liter V-12 that powered Ferrari’s F1 car to six wins in the 1990 season, serves as a stressed member of the chassis. Of course, displacement wasn’t the only thing that the engineers changed. They used variable-length intake runners and a variable exhaust system to make the race engine’s power and torque “more easily accessible,” according to the manufacturer’s[website](https://www.ferrari.com/en-US/magazine/articles/the-f50-a-formula-1-car-for-the-road) , “up to the 8500 rpm redline.” The suspension relied on pushrods and double wishbones at each corner and used electronically controlled Bilstein shock absorbers mounted inboard.

The F50 was hardcore, if you couldn’t tell already: While today a supercar maker might trumpet a stability control system you can completely turn off, the F50 didn’t even have ABS… or power steering or power brakes. Only 349 were made between 1995 and 1997.


Modern exotics are hot right now ([with some exceptions noted here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/data-driven/not-all-modern-exotic-cars-are-hot-right-now/) ), and few are hotter than the F50. Of the 10 highest F50 sales ever, *six* of them occurred in 2026, with the other four in 2025 or 2024. Values for #2 examples are up 102% in 2026 alone. Zoom out to the last six years, and they’re up a whopping 352%.

Broad Arrow Auctions


[Broad Arrow’s example](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/lv26_r0080/1997-ferrari-f50) appears to arrive at an opportune time. Finished in Rosso Corsa over Nero leather with Rosso seat inserts, it is a late-production car (#334), one of approximately 25 examples delivered new to the U.K. It is a remarkably low-mile example, showing just 106 miles from new. The last time we saw an F50 come to market with an odometer reading anywhere close to this figure was in January, when[a 1995 example](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1158440/1995-ferrari-f50/) , also in Rosso Corsa, sold for $12.1M via Mecum. That car displayed 252 miles, or over twice as many as Broad Arrow’s car, which carries an estimate in excess of $20,000,000.

Might we be looking at the next record-selling F50? The low miles are a huge point in favor of this particular car; the[current record holder](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1173405/1996-ferrari-f50/) mentioned at the top of this article had more miles (7500km, or 4660 miles), and sold for $14,575,000. However, that car wore a rarer color, Giallo Modena (yellow).


Whether or not we crown a new king of F50 values in Las Vegas, there is no doubt that the F50 is having a year for the record books, and that this is an exceptional example of a model that’s already ’90s supercar royalty.
